utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Hopefully we will have a good day. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Amongst the Defence teams I notice only the absence -- I notice the absence of only Mr. Haynes. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. The witness is already in his chair. I take it, therefore, that there are no preliminaries. Is there anything wrong with Mr. Haynes or he's just working elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he is not ill. He is healthy and he will join us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And once more, welcome. Mr. Vanderpuye will be proceeding with his examination-in-chief. May I just remind you that you are still -- that the solemn declaration that you made yesterday is still valid today and will continue to be valid throughout your entire testimony, until it is over. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I think yesterday we left off, and you were talking about having gone to Pribicevac and we had just about -- we were talking about the events of the 11th of July, and I was just asking the Court if we could go into private session, so if we could do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, yesterday I made a mistake, an omission, actually, and I would like to explain if you would allow me to do so and it will only take a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. That's what you are here for, to give us the full, correct version of the events. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the 11th of July and my stay in Pribicevac. It is true that on that day I arrived in Pribicevac to see a person very close to me. It is also true that on that occasion I met up with General Mladic and I explained that meeting and I described it. It is true that in Pribicevac I also met with two persons, MD and JM. However, I made a mistake in the sense of speaking about DT. On that day, he was not with me at Pribicevac; he was there two days before, on the 9th. And this is the mistake I made yesterday with regards to that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session so there is no problem in mentioning names while we are in private session. I just want to make sure that we know who you are talking about. Okay. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Witness, for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're still in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Witness. I want to ask you, do you know a person by the name of Tesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I saw that person in Pribicevac, Aleksandar Aco Tesic. He was the chief of the secretariat for national defence in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were in Pribicevac on the 11th, did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aco Tesic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He arrived maybe two hours after me, and he brought people who were doing work obligation. He brought them to Pribicevac. Those were people of military age who had worked in various companies which means that they had not been mobilised into the army, but they had work obligation. He mobilised them and brought them up there, maybe two hours after I got there. We did not get there together, in other words. I came on my own in a vehicle. And then I -- when I was talking about that I made that mistake and I thought that we were talking about the 9th and that's why I mentioned the Dragan Tesic as being there on the 11th. I was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Let's go back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go back into private session. I need to get the names on the record. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I hinted at, but I thought you didn't mind proceeding. So let's go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated certain initials when you were just talking. One was MD. Can you tell us who that is for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session, Witness, so you don't need to worry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You also gave the initials JM. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miodrag Josipovic, the chief of the police station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you also gave the initials DT. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Trisic, assistant commander for logistics of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we go now to open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you met these people in Pribicevac, did you have a prior arrangement to meet them all or was it merely coincidental that you met on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we are not in private session now. Now we are in open session. Just don't mention the names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With MD and JM I had a coincidental meeting. As for AT, I knew I would meet him up there in Pribicevac. In other words, I only knew about AT, that I would meet him there. As for the others, the meeting was purely coincidental.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You indicated earlier that you -- you knew that there was one individual who you met on the 11th that had been up in the -- in that area on the 9th. Can you tell us how you came to know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person that I mentioned as having been there on the 9th of July was not in Pribicevac on the 11th of July and this is where I corrected my yesterday's statement. In other words, DT was not there on the 11th, together with me. He was in Pribicevac two days before, on the 9th of 11 -- of July. That is when we had arranged in Bratunac to go up there. We set up a meeting and we went to Pribicevac together on the 9th. I told you why we had gone there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't want you to read me being finicky, but I am a little bit concerned because, even with the use of the initials, I think if that person is still alive he would be able to identify the witness. Maybe I am being over abundantly cautious, but I would like you to think about it and, if necessary, we will redact it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I agree with the Court's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I wonder what the Defence teams think about it. Because I don't want to overdo it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind if these persons whose initials we're mentioning know that I am testifying. When I asked for protective measures, this was not because of them. In other words, these people can be aware of the fact that I am testifying and that I am mentioning their names or their initials. Have I been of any assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have been extremely helpful, Witness. I think we don't need to redact at this point and we can proceed. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. You indicated yesterday that at a certain point you left Pribicevac. And can you tell us where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I stayed in Pribicevac for about two hours or maybe longer or even shorter. After that I returned to Bratunac, to my office. I went there by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to draw your attention to the 12th of July, if I could. And can you tell us what occurred on that day, as best as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from Pribicevac, as I was sitting in my office, sometime in the afternoon or even in the evening, I met up with DM. He informed me that on the following day at 8.00 I should be at the command of the Bratunac Brigade. And I'm talking about 8.00 on the 12th of July. I did that. I went to work at 7.00, when my working day starts, and from there I went to the command. When I got there they sent me to a room which was in -- on the ground floor and it was used as a meeting room at the command. In that room I saw General Mladic, who was already there. I can't say for a fact who else was there with General Mladic. I know that the Blagojevic, the commander of the brigade, was not there. There may have been some two or three other officers there, I don't know who they were, however. I'm only sure that the -- the General was there. We greeted each other as I entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one thing, just so that the record is clear. In page 7, line 23 of the transcript, there is an indication that you met with DM. And I was just wondering whether DM is MD, and if you could clarify that. I think you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that sometimes I swap the places of the first name and the last name, and I apologise for doing that. It was MD who informed me that evening that on the following morning I should be at that meeting. To my surprise, he himself did not attend that meeting at 8.00. So MD, he had informed me about the meeting, he said that he would be there, but he wasn't. I was the first one to arrive there and the General and some other officers had already been there. As I greeted the General, the General told me, "I don't see you in Srebrenica a lot." And I told him, "General, I have other things to do. I have my everyday work to tend to." Then he offered me a seat. We sat down. And at that moment AT appeared. I have already mentioned him with regard to the events in Pribicevac. And this is what I skipped. While I was there on my own, General talked to me and asked me, "What do you think we should do with the Muslims from Srebrenica?" I was taken by surprise. I asked him, "What do you mean, what you should do?" He said, "Well, Srebrenica has been liberated." So I told him, "Why don't you let them stay at their homes?" And he said, "What if they don't want to stay?" Then I said, "I don't know." I knew that in 1992 they had gone to Tuzla and Kladanj. I told him that we should see what these people wanted at that moment. Then AT appeared and the General asked him the same thing. Maybe two or three minutes later another person appeared and that was the local priest. Again, the General asked him the same question. Maybe I was wrong to mention this, and then LJS appeared and he asked him the same question, and they provided him with almost identical answers as I did, as if we had been in agreement, although none of us knew why we had been invited to the command. We didn't know that the General was waiting for us there and that we would be asked this thing. I spent not more than half an hour at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can I just ask --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, finish your answer and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the half an hour meeting with the General, I did not perceive it as a meeting, actually. I perceived it as something of an informal conversation, i.e., an opportunity for him to inform me to be at the Fontana Hotel at 10.00, for yet another meeting. In other words, my meeting at 8.00, which was not a meeting, was just an opportunity for me to be informed about the meeting that was to take place at 10.00. The General didn't tell us what the agenda of the meeting at 10.00 would be. He just asked us to be there at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, can we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You have indicated another set of initials, this time LJS. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Simic, the president of the Bratunac municipality assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you indicated that you were informed to be at a meeting at 10.00 on the same day. Did you go to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us if, during the course of the meeting, or at the end of the meeting, I should say, if you were given a particular task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 8.00 meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm referring to the 10.00 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the 10.00 meeting? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the four of us who were there at 8.00, only I and LJS were invited to the other meeting at 10.00 and together we went to that meeting at 10.00. The meeting ended, and LJS and I were given a task based on the conclusions of that meeting that we should play a humanitarian role towards the population that was in Potocari. When I say that we had a humanitarian role, I mean that we were asked to provide the population with water, food, medicines, in keeping with our abilities. In Potocari, according to what was said at the meeting, there were some 20.000 people. The day was scorchingly hot; the temperatures were in the 30s. LJS and I were given the task to play the humanitarian role, to be in charge of the water and the food that would be delivered to these people in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, when you were given this assignment, it was only given to the two of you, as you have indicated, out of all of the people that were at the meeting. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only present civilians from the civilian authorities were the two of us and MD.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we just go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that the record is clear, can you just tell us who the people were that were present at that meeting that you recall? And this is the 10.00 meeting, so that...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was attended by General Mladic, General Krstic, the commander of DutchBat, of UNPROFOR, and his deputy. There were two other VRS officers there. I think that they were Colonel -- a colonel and a lieutenant-colonel but I didn't know them, their faces were not familiar. Muslim representatives were also present. It was a three-member delegation, Nuhanovic Ibro, Nesib Mandzic and a woman who is name was Camila. Out of the Muslim delegation I knew Ibro Nuhanovic really well, but Mandzic Nesib, Camila I just knew superficially, but I knew Ibro Nuhanovic well, he was an economist with a degree. He completed his elementary education in Bratunac. Then after the war started, he lived and worked in Bratunac, so we knew each other well. Dragomir Vasic was also there, he was the head of the public security station in Zvornik, and as I said, there was Miroslav Deronjic, Ljubisa Simic and myself as representatives of civilian authority. So that was the attendance at the meeting. The meeting was conducted by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While we are at -- in private session, because my mind is still working on how -- how cautious we have to be, how careful we have to be during the public sessions. The witness said earlier on that he doesn't mind -- he wouldn't mind, but his concerns are rather not focused on the three or four persons that he has mentioned he wouldn't mind them identifying him as testifying again. But at the back of my mind I have this preoccupation: That this gentleman has already testified in Jokic and in Blagojevic, and there will be others that may have or would have followed his testimony then. I speak for myself, but I take it that none of us four have read his testimony in either Blagojevic or Jokic, because we usually don't do that when it's a viva voce witness. But, assuming that he is repeating what he had testified in those two cases without protective measures, I'm not that sure inside that he might not be identified. So I'm going to rely entirely on your good judgement, and you seem to be a very alert witness, sir. If at any moment you feel that we should go into private session, please do let us know and we will. We are in private session at the moment, so do we remain or do we move into open session for the next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can move into open session, but before we do, I just wanted to point out that the subject matter alone of the testimony, read in conjunction with the witness's prior testimony, I think, raises the same concern in any event. And so I am trying to do my best to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no, I rely on your good judgement. If I wasn't assured of that, I mean, I would act differently. But I think I -- we are in good hands, both the witness and you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I make one suggestion, Your Honour, whilst we're in private session. The Court asked the witness exactly what his concerns are, partly because of the expedited nature of the application. It hasn't been dealt with perhaps as fully as it might otherwise be and that might help both the Chamber as well as my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a very good point that you have raised, Mr. Josse. Witness, while we are still in private session, you asked the Prosecution to, in turn, ask for protective measures to be placed in -- to be put in place for you. And we have granted them. What are you really -- what are your real concerns? Why would you want to hide your identity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do. Because it will help us immensely take decisions as we go along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for protective measures for one reason alone. On Saturdays there is a report broadcast in our area called, "The Hague Diary," that's what it's called, and it lasts for half an hour. I cannot remember the journalist, who is a Muslim by ethnicity, and he provides a review of the week in half an hour. And then there are items from different trials, including this trial. Sometimes they -- how can I put it. In one sentence, taken out of context, they present something to the public, and then that takes on a completely different dimension in the area where I live. At the moment, the Srebrenica and Bratunac area is in an upheaval. I don't know if you've heard this proposal that Srebrenica should step out of Republika Srpska. So the political mood is elevated, and I'm afraid that the journalist will take one sentence from my testimony and present it in a negative context and that will reflect negatively upon me in my community. So I asked for protective measures because of the media, because of journalists, not because of the people. What I state here I am going to state that as they say, before God and the people. I have come here to speak the truth, and I am speaking the truth. But I'm afraid of journalists' tricks and that they don't sully my testimony by using a sentence in a particular way in a connotation that may be harmful to me. This is why I sought protective measures. There is no other reason. If you can guarantee to me that no journalist over there would mention me, then I agree that I testify in public. Basically, these are my reasons but, of course, it's up to you to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't give you that guarantee. Ask me something else. But I think we've got a clear picture. Use your good judgement, as I said before. And I thank you, Mr. Josse, for your input. Yes, whenever it's convenient to revert to open session, Mr. Vanderpuye, please, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we're actually in the process of doing that, and that would be fine, if we could go to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the tasks that you were assigned, were you assigned by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of the meeting he said, after all the conclusions were drawn and when it became clear that the Muslims wanted to leave the region, he told us then that you, in the authorities there, should try to help the population up in Potocari. You have filled in all your water cisterns and the bakeries should be working, and after that we withdrew to my office, the three of us, and we made a plan how to continue to operate in this matter. We engaged two of our water cisterns, and a cistern of the utilities company, as well as the fire station cistern. Our local bakery was instructed in future to work in full capacity, and to send all of their produce to the Potocari area. We saw that this was not enough, so then LJS went to the neighbouring municipality across the Drina River, and he asked the authorities there to help us out, which is what they did. They also sent their water cisterns and a certain quantity of bread and juices, mineral water. We did the same with the neighbouring municipality of Zvornik. So they also helped us out there. So these were our capacities that we were able to offer to the people up there. It was probably insufficient, but we didn't have more than that. What we had, we tried to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you actually go to Potocari at some point on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the first cisterns and the first quantities of bread, LJS and I went too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you distribute some of the supplies that you indicated that you had organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, other than the people who were entrusted with the cisterns, there were people from civilian protection, the two of us also participated in handing out bread, milk; there was certain quantities of that. We also tried to help out, literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the meeting itself that happened at 10.00 that day, that began at 10.00 that day, did General Mladic make any indication as to whether or not the people in Potocari would be screened to see if there were any war criminals among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what the purpose of the meeting was when I was informed to attend. At the meeting itself, I understood what the objective of the meeting was. I understood that the meeting was preceded by another meeting with -- can I give the names of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you can, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting, I understood that the General had another meeting with Nesib Mandzic, who at the time was the president of the Srebrenica municipality, and the meeting at 10.00 was attended by the Muslim delegation, actually, a larger Muslim delegation, a three-member Muslim delegation. And I concluded that when the General asked, he addressed the president, President Mandzic, "What have you decided?" To which they replied that they had decided that the people wanted to leave the region. The General warned them, "Don't take such a decision. If you wish to stay in this region, in your homes, you can do that freely, with full guarantees for your rights and freedoms, freedom of work, freedom of movement. And the condition, if you do decide about that, the army must hand over its weapons and those who bloodied their hands and who committed crimes against the Serbian people would be prosecuted. Those who were innocent would have all the guarantees of work, life and movement and they can stay." They were quite decided. "General, thank you very much, but we have decided that we do want to leave this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, approximately how long were you in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you did after you left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I actually physically helped to distribute the bread, the food. And walking around in a kind of narrow circle, some people recognised me. Amongst other people, I was recognised by a man who actually built my house just before the war. His name is Nijazija Jahic. I saw him from about 10 metres off, and he was calling out to me, but I didn't recognise him at the time. And then he came up to me and only when he came up to me I recognised him. I said, "Nijazija, is that you?" He said, "Yes." He asked me if I was able to help him in any way, for him and his wife, if I could get him and his wife into the transport earlier, because the transport had already started. I said, "Yes, I can do that. Where is your wife?" He said, "She's there." I said, "Bring her over," and he brought her over and then the buses were about 200 metres away from where we were, and I took him there and I took them into the bus. And that man, about three years ago, he is now living in Central Bosnia, in Breza or Vares and he sent his greetings via a Serb who is living in Bratunac now. He told him to tell me hello and to thank me for helping him. There was another case when I was recognised by a person by the name of Hamid; he is from the village of Glogova. Before the war, he worked as a messenger in the municipal assembly office. He also asked for my help, to help him to move his uncle, who was in a wheelchair, to also take him into the bus out of turn. Do I need to describe that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before Mr. Vanderpuye tells you whether you need to describe it or not, you have mentioned a lot of names here and a lot of details which, undoubtedly, could reveal your identity, at least to these persons that you mentioned. I'm leaving it in your hands to tell me whether you would like this part to be redacted or whether we proceed. It's up to you. But obviously whoever has heard this will identify you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is not necessary. I am not afraid of anything. I don't think that there is any need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the answer to your question is, no, you don't need to explain that. I think before your answer I'd asked you where -- where you went after you left, and could you tell us, after you left Potocari, where you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac. I don't know if I went to my office or if I went home to refresh myself. It was a very, very hot day, so I'm not sure about that. But I am sure that in the afternoon I was back in my office again, and I spent time in my office in the municipal building. I was there until night. There was another person with me at the office, MD.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we go into private session just to get this person's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You previously -- I'm sorry. Are we in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You previously referred to an individual by the name of MD and now you're referring to MD again. Are you referring to the same individual or is this a different individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the same individual. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other person was Miroslav Deronjic and this person is Dragan Mirkovic, who was sitting at the office with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the director of the Bratunac utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can go into open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that -- well, did this person come to your office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already evening. It could have been after 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did anything occur during the period of time that he was in your office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sitting in the office. I don't know if we had anything we had to do, but anyway, at the time, we did spend a lot of time at the office. Usually the directors would come and meet at my office, so he probably just happened to come by. And we were sitting and talking and then we heard a window was opened, the window to the office, and it looks out to the street and we could hear the sound of some vehicles outside. We looked out of the window and we could see three buses parked on the street right beneath the window. It was strange, what the buses were doing there. We were wondering. Then we stood up and came downstairs; the office is on the first floor. We came down and at the exit to the municipal building there was a bus parked. We could see it was full of people. Men. The front door of the bus was open, and a policeman was standing in front of the door. Judging by his uniform, he was a civilian policeman, not a military policeman. He was wearing a blue uniform, but I didn't know the man. We had a conversation with him, we asked who these people were. He said Muslims. Where are they going, what are they doing here? They are -- and then at one point I noticed that in the middle of the bus a person was knocking on the window, tapping on the window. And the lights in the bus, inside the bus were dimmed. I approached closer and I recognised the person. His name was Omo Jahic and he was from the village of Bijeceva. Before the war he worked at the Sasa mine. He was also a councilman in the municipal assembly, so we knew each other very well. And he asked me to come into the bus. I went back to the policeman, because this was in the middle of the bus, and the policeman was standing at the entrance to the bus. I said, "That man would like to tell me something. Can I go into the bus?" He said, "Go ahead." I climbed the first step, the one close to the driver, and I said, "Omo, what's the matter?" *And he said, "Buco, can you please give me some water, bro?" And since the policeman was right there and the door was open, I said this man wants me to give him some water, can I do that? He said, "Yes, go ahead."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one second. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's redact line 25 on page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The penultimate -- line 25 on page 22, yeah. The penultimate word, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to try to be mindful of what you say. Let me just ask you, because earlier you had indicated that you had asked policemen about these Muslims that were in the buses, and I think you asked the policeman, or you indicated that -- why they were there and where they were going, and I was just wondering if you could tell us if you received an answer to those questions and what he told you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer that I got from the policeman was rather ambiguous. As far as I can remember, he told me that these people would be taken to Batkovic, Bijeljina, to a collection centre, that's what he called it. And from there he would be taken to be exchanged for the Serbian soldiers who were in Tuzla, as well as the Serbian civilian population in Tuzla. This was more or less the answer that the policeman gave me. But I realised that he himself was not very sure of what he was saying when he said that they would be taken to Batkovic and onwards to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, during the course of that evening, approximately how many buses you became aware of had come in to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: MD and I saw two buses and we brought about 50 cans of water to those two buses. Everybody on those two buses had small, five-litre cans, and we also saw in the other street, on the other side of the municipal building, there were three more buses parked. In other words, there were three buses on one side and three buses in front of the municipality building; six buses in total. There were also buses in the playground. I didn't go there, but according to some stories, there must have been anything between 20 and 25 buses, or 20, approximately. *Q. Now, did the number of buses and the Muslims on those buses create a situation of concern for -- for you as the -- as the president of the Executive Board of the municipality of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now you have cooked --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was very nicely done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise for that. Maybe we can redact that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if we can get it right this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that create a situation of concern in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, rumours reached me that in the buses that were in the playground something strange was going on. That the Muslims in those buses were shouting to each other, and there was a fear that they might get off the buses. Since there were very few guards providing security for those buses, I'm concluding that there were very few guards because there was just one policeman for the three buses in front of the municipal building. That's why there was a fear that the Muslims would leave the buses and start walking around the town, which was empty. In the town there was no troops, there were no males. There were mostly women, children and the elderly. As for the able-bodied men, they were either in the army or hiding in the forest. The retired persons were sent to the playground in order to create an impression that there were more guards than there actually were. And the drivers were ordered to start the engines, to keep the engines running, in order to prevent people in the buses from communicating to each other. These buses spent the night in Bratunac, and in the course of the night, before the morning, they left Bratunac. I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you become aware at some point, during that evening or the following morning, as to what -- as to whether or not some of these individuals were being brought to a school located near the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I realised that there were many buses in Bratunac, I came across MD in town, but not the person who shared the office with me, but the first one. I don't know whether you are all clear as to who I'm referring to. And I told him, "Man, what is this? What is going on? Where did the buses come from?" He responded, "RD from M has done this to us."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we can go into private session and we can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe you can explain that to us, just so that it's clear for the record. You can use their names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what he literally said. "Rajko Dzukic from Milici is framing us up." And then he left. Then I told him, "Miroslav, use your connections, talk to somebody from the top leadership." Because he did have some connections with the political and the state leadership, which I didn't have. So I asked him to inquire into the matter, and prevent all that. I thought that we didn't need all this, and this is how it ended between the two of us. He promised that he would see to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You had indicated an MD is the person that you were speaking to, right -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, could you just tell us his name now that we're in private session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can go to open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I had asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I had asked you whether or not you had become aware of the use of the school with regard to some of these individuals that were on the buses. Did that occur at any point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this happened on that evening, but on the following day I learned that, early in the morning, people had been detained in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you had some certain information that there were -- I think you said that there were some buses near the playground. Now, do you know whether or not there were people outside the buses, that is Muslims, outside the buses on the playground, or were they all on the buses, if you have that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all on the buses. According to my information, nobody was outside. Possibly, if somebody lost their way, Potocari is only five kilometres away, and there 20.000 people there. We learnt later on that some people went astray from Potocari and strayed into Bratunac and then they were brought to the school. I did not see the school as a prison, I saw it as a collection centre at the time, because the school had been destroyed in 1992, all the glass panes were shattered. It did have walls and a roof, but as any other school, this also had a lot of windows, a lot of glass panes which were all shattered in 1992, and from then on it was never used by children. There was another school nearby that was used by children as a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If I could, I'd like to just move forward and we'll go into the 13th of July. I will direct your attention to that day. Now, did you, at some point during that day, go to see -- I think DT is who you've referred to this individual as before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in the morning I went to see DT.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he provide you with any information with respect to a former head of the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: DT was an associate of mine. We worked very well together. He was also a personal friend, and we went to school together. That's why we socialised quite a lot. That morning I went to see him, to have a cup of coffee with him and to have a chat. I wanted to be informed about war operations and so on. When I arrived there he told me, "Do you know who has been detained?" I said, "Who?" And I can tell you his name, if I may. That person who -- who had been detained. Resic Imanovic [as interpreted] is his name. Resic Imanovic is a person who between 1980 and 1984 was the chief of the Bratunac police. And during the same period of time I was his deputy, which means that we worked together in the police station. In addition to the two of us having worked together, that person was also a very good friend of mine. We were really close, our families were close. We were really good pals. We spent all of our free time together, either sitting in a cafe or fishing together. We were really close. I expressed a wish to see Resid, so he told me he is down there, by ZC.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just stop you right there for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you move further. He has -- you asked him questions, and he answered them in relation to the school. And to my knowledge the only indication that he gave as to which school he was referring to is when, on page 25, line 20, he said, "To a school located near the municipal building." Later on he has mentioned another school without mentioning the name, of course. So I think we need to clarify this, if either or both of these schools had a name, perhaps he can give us the name of the schools and that would make his testimony clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe -- I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- for interrupting but maybe we need to redact something. If I can draw your attention at page -- one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you're referring to page 28, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: 28, yes. Yes. 20 to 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know of course as he was saying it, I have been thinking all along, actually, I think his entire testimony could fall under that category. But in referring, or when referring to this gentleman, Resid, you said -- you gave some information about how close you were to him, which could identify you. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- do you wish us to redact that or not? Because at the end of the day, the conclusion I'm coming to is the only purpose of the protective measures that we have put in place is to the effect that whoever will eventually identify him in any case is precluding -- precluded from revealing his identity. That's the only purpose. But I don't think that we are moving in the direction of hiding his identity. I think we've had too much information in public session, in open session, that would reveal his identity to many. Do you wish us to redact that part or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is a well-known fact. Everybody knows that I met up with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, in any case, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First I think -- first I'd like to see if we can address the Court's concern with respect to the name of the school. And you had referred to the school, or having learned that certain people were brought to a school, and I am wondering if you could give the name of the school as it was during that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion, the school that is in the vicinity of the municipal building, before the war, it's name was Vuk Karadzic. During the war, however, its name was changed and it was given the name of Branko Radicevic. Whereas the Vuk Karadzic name was given to the school whose name was Hasan Midhat before the war. In other words, the school next to the municipal building that the detainees were brought to was called Branko Radicevic at the time. Am I making myself clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very much so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can we just go to private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had referred to somebody I think earlier in your testimony with the initials of ZC. And I wondered if you could just give us that person's name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zlatan Celanovic. So not C, but C-h. He worked in the military police as an investigator. He was not a commander, he was an investigator. He had a law degree. He investigated, he interviewed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at some point, did you actually have an opportunity to meet and to talk to Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called Dragan Trsic, DT, that is, asking if he would want to see him as well. He said no, but I wanted to see him. We had been pals, we had worked together. So he said, why don't you call ZC, you have a telephone there, and ask him. I dialed his number and I asked ZC, I understand that Resid is in custody. And he says, yes. Can I see him? Yes. When? You can see him immediately. So I said, Okay, I'm coming over there. The military police building is only 30 or four [as interpreted] metres away from the place where I was with DT. It's very close to the command. So I got to ZC's office very quickly; he was there alone. And then he went out and a minute or two later he brought Resid into his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session. Any time you wish to go back to open session, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can go back into open session, but I just wanted to clarify for the record, I may have eaten my words, but with respect to page 31, at line 19, the name that I thought I said was Sinanovic, not Celanovic. That's what's reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript needs to be corrected, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Sinanovic, S-i.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we go into open session, or shall we remain in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can go to open session, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go to open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to speak to Resid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As Resid entered the office, I could tell by the expression on his face that Zlatan hadn't told him that he would meet up with me, so I was taken by surprise when he saw me in that office. I stood up, came up to him, we shook hands. We greeted each other. For some 10 seconds or so, he held my hand and then we even kissed each other. We sat down at a coffee table that was in the office. Zlatan had left the office. He left us alone for an hour or even longer. We spent that time talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you receive any information as to what would be done with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as I was glad to see him, I was still embarrassed, because I couldn't help him. I didn't have the power to take him out and tell him, "You can go, you're free." And I wanted him to be aware of that. I told him, "Resid, whatever is being done, this is a purely military operation. I work in the municipality." And he said, "I know. I know all. I heard it on the radio." They could listen to the radio up there in Srebrenica. "I heard it on the radio when you had been appointed and I would like to thank you as a human being, as a person, for having come to see me." I asked him, "Resid, did somebody ill-treat you? Are you hungry?" And he said, "No, nobody did, and I'm not hungry." And then we continued chatting, talking about things, maybe for an hour or so. But I wanted to encourage him; this was my intention. And I told him, "Don't fret. You will be exchanged." Because this is what I had been told by DT and that's what all of us had believed. I told Resid, "You will be exchanged. I don't expect any problems with that." I tried to help Resid in 1992. I remember the date very well. Because this had all happened on the 6th of May, on the eve of St. George's Day, which is my name day. That's why I remember the date very well. On the 5th of May, on the eve that holiday, sometime in the afternoon, Resid called me on the phone at my place and asked me to come and fetch him in his apartment, which I did. In the apartment I found him, his wife, and their two sons. We greeted each other of course, and then he told me right away, "You know why I called you? I called you because something smells really odd in Bratunac. I would like to go to Skopje, to my brother's." His brother Iza was a captain in the JNA. "I want to go there while things are the way they are and then I'll come back when things settle down. I was going to ask you, maybe you could apply for my pass to leave Bratunac." Since my neighbour, my first-door neighbour was in charge of that, I told Resid, "I believe I can help you." Although at the time, I was not a member of the SDS. I was a member of the SDP, the former communist party, the league of communists. So I was not of the same political mind as MD, but we were neighbours, we were close. That's why I went to see MD. I couldn't find him right away. I found him only around 9.00 in the evening at a meeting, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, is this part of the discussion that you had with him on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Resid, "When I provided you with that pass, why didn't you leave? Why didn't you go to Skopje?" Because if he had gone to Skopje, he would not have been in Srebrenica. And he said, "I made a mistake. I should have left on the 6th." Because on the 6th, in the morning, I gave him the passes. But he didn't leave on the 6th, he left on the 7th. He had a very small car at the time. He had a small Fiat. And Skopje is far away, so he thought that he would first go to Bjelevac, some five kilometres from Bratunac and then on the 7th he was going to leave to Skopje to have a whole day ahead of him. However, on the bridge of the Drina, he crossed to Serbia, and came to Ljubovija, which is some three kilometres away from the bridge on the Drina. And up there, by the motel, the Serbian police from Ljubovija stopped him and ordered him to go back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a good time for the break. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, after you left ZC, C-h, did you return to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after seeing him, yes. I briefly went back to DT, we exchanged a few sentences, and then in 10 or 15 minutes, I returned to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, after you went back to Bratunac, did you at any point after that, go to any school in relation to Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked ZCh how long Resid would stay there. He said, "In the afternoon I will have to transfer him to the elementary school, Branko Radicevic." He said that our police was over there, that's what he said. And I'm going to tell the policemen to take special care of Resid, so that nobody mistreats him. And, having heard that our police were securing the school over there, I also passed down that street near the school, because it's the same way, either to take that road or the main road to the municipal building, and in front I saw a policeman, in front of the school, whom I knew. And I told him, if they bring Resid there, that he should take care of him a bit, if he should need water and so on, so that nobody mistreats him. That was the only time that I went to the school or passed by the school. But the school actually is about 100 metres from the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, if you could, could you just describe that school and any adjacent buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a three-storey building, the school building. I used to be a teacher myself, and I know that the school has 16 classrooms; it's a large school. And it also has a gym. Near the school, as I said, is the municipal building, some 50 to 75 metres away. There is also the old secondary school centre. It's an old building, the old building of the construction school. There was also a hangar there that was dilapidated and that was used as a workshop by the secondary school centre before the war. On the other side are private houses, close to the school. This is a brief description of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I want to draw your attention to the 14th of July, 1995, if I could. Now, were you working on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From 7.00 onwards, perhaps a few minutes before, but actually the work hours were from 7.00 a.m., that's when I would usually get to work. So on the 14th, I came to my office at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while you were at your office, did anybody visit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it was at 7.00 or a few minutes after 7.00, two people came to my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go into private session for a moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just tell us the names of the -- or the name of the people or person who came to visit you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was Jovan Nikolic, and the other one was Dragan Nikolic. Jovan Nikolic was a director of the cooperative, and Dragan Nikolic was also a director of the cooperative. How can I explain that organisation? In the Bratunac municipal region, there were several cooperatives and they were joined, or associated in an organisation which was called the complex cooperative organisation. The cooperative in Kravica was part of this complex cooperative. I cannot be sure, but at that time there was a kind of break-up, and this association fell apart, so I cannot really be sure whether it was Jole or Dragan Nikolic who was the director of the Bratunac cooperative. It was on the cusp of Dragan Nikolic going -- outgoing as director and Jovan Nikolic being appointed. So we were just talking about what had happened the previous afternoon, what happened in the afternoon in the cooperative in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we can go to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've indicated that you had a discussion with these individuals that came to see you about Kravica. Can you tell us what it is that they told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that the day before, in the afternoon, there were killings of Muslims in the cooperative. Until then I hadn't heard of that. The first I heard of it was from them and it surprised me very much; I was flabbergasted. I couldn't believe it. I couldn't believe that something like that had happened. Especially because I had been present at the meeting at the Fontana, where it was agreed that there would be an evacuation, that it would all be done properly. And then suddenly there is this. It had a devastating effect on me. I was shocked. I couldn't believe it. Unfortunately, it was true, and it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At some point after your conversation with these individuals, did you get a call to go to the SDS offices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conversation with those two was just a conversation and getting information. I don't know why they came to tell me that. I assume that it was because they knew -- well, they came to see me frequently, and they probably felt the need to tell someone, to discuss it with someone. So perhaps, after two hours after the conversation with them they told me about it, they stayed with me for an hour or so, I can't be quite certain about that. But then sometime after that, at 9.30 or thereabouts, the secretary of the Serbian Democratic Party called me. She asked me if she could come to the office. She asked me if I could go to the office because there was a man waiting there to see me. I said I would go there, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what happened when you went to the office? First, did you meet this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went to the office. When I entered the office I saw the secretary there, and also a male. The secretary was sitting at her desk, and the person was sitting at the coffee table. When I entered, the person addressed me. They shook my hand. I didn't know that person before, it was the first time that I saw him. He introduced himself. And he offered me a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What did he tell you his name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Beara. As soon as I saw "Colonel Beara" on the uniform. So I was there with him for 10 minutes at the most. It was an informal conversation: "How are you, what's going on? How is it in Bratunac? How are you dealing with all the work?" And so on. So, as I said, it was an informal conversation, from what I can recall of it. The SDS offices actually had two rooms, there were two offices. The first one is the office where the secretary was sitting and where the Colonel was and then there is an entrance to the other office. It's like a leather-covered, padded door. And that's where the office was where the president sat. And the Colonel told me, "Will you come to the other office? There are some people there who would like to talk to you." He didn't tell me who these people were or what they wanted to talk about with me. I stood up, I opened the door, I entered that office, and there I saw two officers whom I didn't know. In uniforms. I think that one of them was a colonel and the other one was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not -- whether or not these individuals were members of the brigade, Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not. They were not definitely members, because I knew all of the members of the Bratunac Brigade, and these people I was seeing for the first time. If I saw them now, I wouldn't recognise them. Because I had never seen them before, they didn't introduce themselves, they didn't tell me their names. And they were not from the Bratunac Brigade. That, I'm 100 per cent sure. Because I knew people from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the Colonel about who these people were, or might have been?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never met the Colonel again. Not when I was leaving. I didn't ask him who these people were. After finishing the conversation with those people, I left the SDS, I said good-bye to the Colonel, I didn't comment anything with him, we didn't really talk about what happened inside with these other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what transpired, what the conversation was -- you had with these other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people very quickly moved to the question of why they had called me over to see them. They asked me, "What do your -- the companies in your municipality have of construction equipment, machinery?" I said that our brickworks had a construction machine called a ULT, and the utilities company had a smaller machine called a SKIP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just describe what those machines are, so we're clear on the record what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ULT machine is a construction machine. I'm not an expert in construction, but I can describe it as well as I can. It has a large bucket, it's a large machine. And I think it's used for loading. I don't think, I know it's used for loading. And it has a large bucket. Perhaps the size of that desk or maybe a bit smaller. The SKIP machine is owned by the utilities company and it is used for digging. It is a very small piece of machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you do anything in relation to -- to getting these machines or providing these people with access to those machines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked if we would be able to place the ULT machine at their disposal, and I said that I think so, yes, and that I would call the director of the brickworks, whose name was NN.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could just go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedzo Nikolic, the director of the brickworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While we're in private session, did you call anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time that you were in this meeting with these two other individuals, a colonel and lieutenant-colonel, was -- was Colonel Beara in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel -- the Colonel stayed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we remain in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, we can go to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: During the time you were in the meeting with these two other individuals, the colonel and lieutenant-colonel, was Colonel Beara in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Colonel Beara stayed in the first office where the secretary was sitting. Actually, that was where I found him when I came in. He didn't come into this other office where I was with the other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you at any point discuss the subject matter of that meeting with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Colonel did not tell me, when I came, why I had been summoned over. And when I came out, he didn't ask me, "Did you make any kind of agreement? What did you agree on?" As they would say, we didn't discuss work, if I can put it that way. We didn't discuss the reasons why I had been summoned to come over. Perhaps it's interesting also to say this: When those people told me about the machinery, that they needed it, I had an idea why they would need the machine. And the previous meeting I had with these two, JN and ND, kind of clued me in about why they would need the machinery, that that's why they would need the machinery, for that sort of thing. Remembering 1992 and the person who operated the machine, that person is my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Sorry for the interruption, but we needed to discuss something before the witness finished answering the question. So you were saying, Witness, that perhaps it's interesting also to note this, when those people told me about the machinery, that they needed it, I had an idea why they would need the machine. And the previous meeting I had with these two, JN and ND, kind of clued me -- gave me a clue about why they would need the machinery. And that's why they would need the machinery, for that sort of thing. And you were going to explain when I interrupted you. If you could continue from there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we misunderstood each other. In that context, these two others that I first met have nothing to do with these other two, but when they informed me about what had happened, I myself formed a kind of assumption about why they would be needing this machine. So I hope that's clear. I started to talk about the man who was operating the machinery. I knew him. And I know that in 1992 he had an unpleasant experience while operating the machinery, doing the kind of work that I had an idea that the machine was needed for. So I told the people, "You will get the machine for sure, but the person who operates the machine is not for that sort of thing." And then one of the two men actually told me very sharply, "It's not up to you to say who can work on the machine and who cannot." And I said, "I'm sorry, it was just a remark and it doesn't oblige you to anything." And then I withdrew from the office with the promise that the machine would be placed at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you discuss with either of these men, in this meeting, your concern, or your idea, as to what use those machines would be put?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which people? The people at 7.00 in the morning or these officers, army officers? I don't know who you mean. I don't know which ones you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I mean the officers, the later -- the later of the two meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers didn't tell me why they would be needing the machine. It was my assumption that they would possibly need it for that, or perhaps for some kind of combat action, digging trenches or something. But having heard about what had happened in Kravica, I thought to myself that perhaps that's why it would be needed. But they didn't tell me what the machine would be used for, that machine. I wasn't told what it would be used for. That was my assumption. And it was my attempt to protect the man who kept fainting in 1992, when he was doing this kind of hard work with that machine. But I said don't take that for anything, it was just an assumption, it doesn't commit anyone to anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the manner in which these men approached you with respect to acquiring that equipment, was that the common way of proceeding normally between civilian and military relations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: In the Blagojevic case, there was debate about that; how you can get a machine. There were three ways to get the equipment. First, you can get it through the secretariat for national defence to requisition the machine. The command of the Bratunac Brigade could address -- could directly address the Executive Board, but the command could also address the director directly. In this case, they, the people whom I didn't know, these officers, asked me, *as the president of the Executive Board. There was no written request, just an oral request, and I've already told you where that was and how the usual way to do it, since the Bratunac Brigade communicated, or DT, the logistics deputy, was the one who would do these kinds of things directly with us. I mean, he was authorised to do that by the commander, but this time, this is how it happened. Perhaps it's a little bit out of the ordinary. Perhaps this was the most unusual way to do it. Everything else would be more regular, either to go through the secretariat or through the Bratunac Brigade, but this time it didn't go like that, it went like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did that strike you as unusual? Had you been put in a position like this before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I understood it was war, and some things probably do not proceed according to the rules or the law. I mean, perhaps there is no time for certain things. Some things, well, also were done in a roundabout way, perhaps not according to procedure and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go into private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had mentioned that you were concerned about the operator of this ULT equipment. And you said that you knew him, and I would like for you to just put his name on the record so that we know who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jurkovic [as interpreted], I cannot remember his first name. I know the person. Durkovic. He was here, he testified in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not all right as yet. All right. Okay. We are in private session, but one needs to be careful because I don't know whether that person was a protected witness in the Blagojevic case or not. So at the moment, now we switch back to open session. The witness needs to be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go back to open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Let's go back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated that this individual you were concerned about because he kept fainting in relation to an operation in 1992. Could you just tell us what it was that he was doing?
