utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I was exaggerating a little bit saying that I was concerned or worried. It wasn't that I was overly concerned; I just wanted to spare the man of that. He was digging graves for the burial of Muslims who were killed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that the idea that you had that the equipment would have been used for in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that. This is what I thought, as I heard this from MJ and ND at 7.00. This was my assumption. I kept thinking to myself that the machine might be needed for similar things, and that's why I wanted to protect the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But nobody ever told me why the machine was actually needed. This was just my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you very much, Witness. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, if you are leaving that, as to what happened in Kravica warehouse, although he said he was flabbergasted or shocked and it had a devastating effect on him, he didn't give much of a description of what he heard from those two gentlemen. So if you could get as far as you can, the verbatim description of what they told to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's concern or question regarding to the information that you received concerning Kravica. Can you be more specific or as specific as you can, I should say, with respect to the information that was conveyed to you by these two gentlemen that you met at 7.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that on the 13th, in the afternoon, in a brutal way, several hundreds of Muslims had been killed. I can't remember the exact number, but I believe that the figure that they had mentioned was some 600 or 700 people. I tried to create a picture, being aware of the size of that area, and I was shocked to hear that so many people could be squeezed into such a small place and to be killed there. I didn't go to see that, but according to their words, the corpses were on top of each other in a very small room, some six to 700 people had been killed there. Later on various figures were mentioned and I don't believe that the truth has ever been found out. Nobody knows whether the number of people killed were 500 or a thousand, but I believe that the picture was terrible, that the killings had been committed by various tools or rifles, hand-grenades, whatnot, all sorts of weapons. Even they, these two men, when they had arrived to see all this, that they saw some unknown men, people that they didn't know. And at one point arms were drawn against these two people who had introduced themselves as being the managers of that combine, then these people who were committing the crimes cursed them and ordered them to get away. There were some peasants who had their houses in the vicinity who were also shouted at, an elderly person who resided there who is godfather to one of the two, a very old and senile person. He also was shocked and everybody else in the vicinity who were passing by. It was a terrible thing. I can't even begin to describe how it was. I myself didn't see it, but according to them, it was just atrocious. It was terrible, it was devastating. It was shocking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you just tell us, did they provide you any information as to the state of the area at the time that they came to see you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what area are you referring to. The building is on the very road from Bratunac to Kravica and further on to Konjevic Polje. It is some 10 kilometres [as interpreted] from the asphalt road, there is a fence, and you can actually see it on the road. It's actually 10 metres from the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is the condition of the building at the time that they came to see you in the sense of whether or not it had been cleaned up or was in the process of being cleaned up or anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing had been done. They did ask me what we should do. I said nothing, we are powerless. It's up to the army. The army knows what to do, we're not supposed to interfere. This is not our job. So we did not arrive at any conclusions as to do something, that we should do something. This was just information, but we did not act upon it. We didn't know what to do. It was just information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you very much, Witness. I don't have any further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Who is going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'll be the first to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I am a bit confused about the process of going into private session or remaining in open session. I will try and be cautious and avoid the danger of making a mistake in light of what has been happening so far, but let me apologise in advance. When we are talking about the 11th of July, 1995, yesterday you stated that on that day you were in a village called Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity, was there the command post of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was not the command post of the Bratunac Brigade; it was the command post of the 3rd Battalion, i.e., up there, this was the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Battalion. I suppose that this was also the command -- I wouldn't know. I'm not sure. It was called a command post, but whether this was the command post of the 3rd Battalion or the Bratunac Brigade, I wouldn't be sure of that. I believe that Colonel Blagojevic who was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was not there. Maybe General Krstic was there at that command post. Maybe this was also the command post of the corps, I don't know. I'm not sure. In any case, Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, was not there. This was referred to as a command post, and I know that General Krstic was there. From the place where I was, where -- am I -- am I -- am I going too far? I apologise. Am I saying too much?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to answer my questions. I don't have much time. Just please be very concise and straightforward. A person very close to you was there, if I understood you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some 200 or 250 metres away from the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander to you and that person very close to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What commander? Was it Colonel Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: As you've told us, you had a very unpleasant encounter with General Mladic. When was the next time when you saw General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the following morning, on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And this is the event that you described as having taken place at the command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you well, it was MD who invited you to come to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: MD. But he himself did not appear at that meeting. MD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And who told you that you were supposed to be at the 10.00 meeting at Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic told me, and LJS that, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 2D81? Page number 3 in B/C/S, please. I will kindly ask the witness to read that part. Therefore, I would like us to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the English version, but that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: This is your interview that you provided to the investigators of the OTP on the 28th of February. Do you remember, did you talk to Mr. Ruez on 28th February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. It was on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Pale, yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were doing fine, but you are now moving a little bit too fast. So if you could allow a short pause between question and answer, please. Witness, this is important because we have interpreters who need to translate to us into English and French what you are saying in the Serbo-Croat language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to point to you line 19. You were discussing the organisation of that meeting in the Hotel Fontana on the 12th of July, 1995. Could you please read the question that starts in line 19. The initials JR are the initials of Mr. Ruez, and he's asking you something. Can you please read line 19? Maybe I can read it to you. It says, "How were you informed that --"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in front of me. Thank you. Yes, I have it. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Line 21 that you can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says I was informed by Deronjic. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: You say here that it was Deronjic who informed you. Can you tell us who Deronjic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Miroslav Deronjic was the president of the local SDS, and I believe that at that time President Karadzic had appointed him as the civilian commissioner for Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Enough. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: To the investigator's question, you answered that Miroslav Deronjic informed you that you should attend that meeting. Here you say that General Mladic told you that you were supposed to attend the meeting. I would like to clarify that. Can you clarify this for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and clarify this. I did not mention the meeting at 8.00 at the command of the Bratunac Brigade in this interview. I didn't mention it because I did not consider this 8.00 encounter as a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: This is not what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish a link. That's why I said that Deronjic had informed me. It was Deronjic who had informed me about that 8.00 meeting. Deronjic himself did not appear for that 8.00 meeting and when I was providing this interview to Mr. Ruez, I did not find it important to make a distinction. Deronjic did not [as interpreted] come at 8.00, but he did come at 8.00 and I did not see it as very important who was it who informed me about the 10.00 meeting. But now I know. I know that it is important because Deronjic had not appeared at the command at 8.00 and he had informed me about the 8.00 meeting. It was only logical that it could have been only General Mladic who could inform me about the 10.00 meeting. That's why I never said to Mr. Ruez that it was General Mladic who informed me about that meeting because, at the time, I did not deem that to be important. The fact that either one or the other informed me about the meeting is something that I didn't deem important. The most important thing for me was that I attended the meeting and it is only now that I realise that it does make a difference. This is my explanation. You have to bear in mind that this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify this thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I make myself clear now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the 12th of July. You said that in the evening you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we remain in private session or can we move in open session now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: On the 12th, in the afternoon and in the evening, you were in the your office, as far as I understood you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And you had a visitor, a visitor with initials DM?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we talked shop. It was a casual thing; we did not have an agenda. We were chatting, we were probably drinking coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about the situation in Potocari, since you had been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it was an unavoidable subject. There was war, and I'm sure that we discussed war operations. We compared notes. It is only logical that we spoke about that. But there was no protocol to that. It wasn't on any agenda because there was no agenda. It was -- I mean, we could have easily been sitting in a cafe and discussed the same things. But we didn't. We were sitting in the office, we had a telephone there, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When you went to see what was happening in front of the municipal building, did that person go with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And was that person helping the people who were in the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with me. As much as I helped, they helped too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And when you received information that the buses were at the pitch, the field, what I understood you is that there was a possibility that the situation would be unsafe. You said that old-age pensioners were sent there to create a kind of impression there. Who sent them? Who ordered it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot be sure about that. I didn't order it. So I wasn't the one who said they sent the old-age pensioners there. I don't know whether this was done by the police station that is close by the playing field and that is responsible for the security and the law and order in town anyway, but somebody did it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: My next question is, how do you know that this was done? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it. I don't know who told me. I really cannot speculate now. I just want to be to the point and brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I -- from what I understood from your testimony, is that you met that evening, the person with the initials MD?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And that you asked him what was happening and that he told you that there was a certain person from a certain place, that they planted this on him, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was his reaction to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, the person who is from this other place, is that a person from the military structures or the civilians structures? Who is that person? What do they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person is from civilian structures with a lot of influence in the community where he lived and broader.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If you can explain a little bit how you understood that, that that person was creating or planting this situation for the people in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. It's not clear to me why MD used that expression, it's a little bit vulgar. I'm not sure why that person MD used that term, to plant something, to frame someone. Probably thinking that they wanted to protect their own place. That's why they were pushing that transport to Bratunac, to avoid any kind of mess in his own town and he used his influence to do that to Bratunac, so that was MD's view, his opinion. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to clarify one more situation about the school, because there was something unclear about the school. Is it the same school where Muslim prisoners were placed in 1991 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can correct the transcript. It is 1992 and not 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It will be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, 1995, you described all the things that were happening, and you described a certain conversation that you had with other persons and a conversation with Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time that Resid Sinanovic was suspected of some war crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I let him know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the person who allowed you to go and visit Resid Sinanovic actually questioned him or interrogated him about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And that he was interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was suspected of a crime because Sinanovic told me that when I asked him, "Resid, why didn't you escape from Srebrenica over the Drina to Tara just like many other Muslims did and surrendered to the Red Cross of Serbia. And then they were accommodated safely there." He said, "I meant to do that, but I was in touch with -- with my brother in Skopje through the radio."

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't need to tell us the whole story. Maybe you can just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivanisevic's book had already been published in which it was stated that Resid Sinanovic and Sinanovic's family was a family of war criminals and he found out that Enzic's job is that, he is an investigator and an interrogator in the military police and that's how I know that. Enzic told me about it himself, that he had talked with him. *Q. You also testified in the Blagojevic case and again you described today three ways to requisition material and equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that actually the only legal way is to requisition the equipment through the defence ministry of Republika Srpska, which is then -- which then sends the request to the local authorities? *These three ways that you described today, it is not said anywhere, and you yourself didn't mention that one of the ways to go was to go through the Executive Board. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll leave it in your hands to redact, okay. Let's proceed. She knows exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me now if the legal way is the one that I explained? First of all, do you agree with me that that is the legal way to do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that is the legal way, and I also agree that perhaps I did not adhere to procedure, but it was wartime. Some things are done summarily, so perhaps this was done in this case too, that procedure was respected, but it was done the way it was done. *And I want to say that I'm not a lawyer, I'm a teacher, so I'm not really all that versed in laws and regulations. I was just going along with things by inertia. After all it was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are taking care of some redactions. In the meantime, you can proceed. But please be careful, both of you. If you want to know what we are redacting we can tell you, but you can trust our judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The situation is a little bit unclear to me. You are not a lawyer. It's a time of war, war conditions, and you are performing a certain function. Did you have any lawyer that you were able to consult with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear to me that not knowing the regulations can lead to harm, but at the time, I didn't think that was necessary. I did have someone like that, but I didn't think it was necessary. I could have consulted -- I was perhaps caught unawares with the speed of things and the request. I agree that I failed to adhere to procedure, but I don't believe that I did anything wrong. That's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you know why I'm asking you that? I'm asking you that because now, today, in your testimony, you told about the first meeting that you had on the 14th of July, 1995, where you were informed that something terrible had happened, and you said that yourself, in Kravica. After that, you had a meeting, an hour and a half later or an hour and a bit later, and you then find yourself in a situation in the way that you described. So it's a little bit unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You call that a meeting? As far as I was concerned, it was just part of my ongoing, daily duties. I have meetings like that every day; tens of meetings like that, a conversation of 10 or 15 minutes. It's not a scheduled meeting. As far as I'm concerned, that is just my daily work, ongoing, regular duties. And this meeting at the SDS was not something that I considered to be a meeting, but just something that was ongoing. A conversation that took place, I was there for 20 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can call that whatever you like, a working meeting, a meeting, an encounter. The fact is that, according to your testimony, two men who you don't know asked you to provide certain material and equipment, and that you, beforehand, were aware that something had happened. So my question is why, in that situation, did you not respect the procedure, and if you were not familiar with the procedure, why didn't you consult a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know. I did not. Why I didn't, I don't know. Ten or 12 years since then, I don't know why I didn't -- I don't know if there was time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered this question on -- more than once already. So let's move to the next item, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If it's not a problem, I would also like to ask you about this situation with two men who are absolutely unknown to you. Did they consult -- did you consult the Bratunac Brigade about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them in what capacity they were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twelve years later, you're asking a lot of me. My memory since then has faded a lot. I told you "no" in response to your previous two questions, but perhaps I did. What I remember was that I did not. Perhaps they told me that they were from the corps, but I don't remember that now. But let's say that they did not say that, or that they were not. I really cannot say now, after 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: All right. You remember, you don't remember, very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them why they needed the machinery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I said that already, that I had an idea for myself why they needed the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that, after 12 years, memory fades. Does that also imply that the events that are more recent are fresher in your recollection? Why am I asking that? I am asking you that because you talked with Mr. Ruez three years after that event, less than three years after that, and you told Mr. Ruez, an investigator of the OTP, nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't ask me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness Exhibit 2D81. In Serbian, it's page 14, lines 33 and 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If you look at Mr. Ruez's question, which begins on line 33, where he says, "So, during July, 1995, you have no knowledge of there being a need for mass burials of victims or other persons?" It's a very direct question. On the next page, on page 15, line 1, there is your answer. And your answer is negative, that you didn't have any information, you practically just said "no." But this implies that you didn't have any information about there being any need for mass burials of victims or other persons. So Mr. Ruez asked you directly about this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he was asking me about Serb burials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Why did you think that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought. I don't know why I thought that. But at that time, that's what I thought, that he was asking about those burials. Because we were dealing with burials of Serbian victims directly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I really don't want to listen about 1993, the number of people then. This is a very direct question. And my direct question is about July of 1995 and the mass burial of victims and other persons. And your answer was "no." In other words, this was not about Serbs, about a different period, for example, 1993, no. This is about July 1995, and you provided a negative answer. My question to you is this: Can you explain why did you say to Mr. Ruez that you didn't know anything about the need to bury --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered the question already, Mr. Mrkic. Move to your next question. Once he gives you an answer, unless it's an unclear answer, you should proceed to the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that I didn't understand Ruez completely. If that was his goal, he could have asked me some subquestions. He could have clarified a little. I misunderstood his question. I said "no." If he hadn't been satisfied, maybe he should have asked me additional questions so as to make it absolutely clear what he wanted. In this case, my answer would have been different. But he did not lead me properly in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Since we're talking about that, *I suppose that you remember your *evidence in the Blagojevic case, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I don't know what you're referring to. *Q. You were asked the same thing in the Blagojevic case, and your answer was that at the time you did not believe this to be at all important. I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you now that Ruez also didn't think that this was important. If it had been important to him, he would have continued, ask me questions along the same line. I don't...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are taking care of the redactions. Don't worry. Go ahead. But if, possible, please, you could refrain from referring to certain events that could expose his identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the conversation that you had with Mr. Ruez when you spoke about the meeting that took place in the early morning hours of the 14th of July when you were told about the events that had taken place in Kravica? Did you ever mention that to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a document? Is there a transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a transcript of that interview. There is a recording of that interview. I can provide it to you during the break. But I didn't find it anywhere.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I didn't mention it then. If it's not in the transcript, then I didn't mention it. If I had mentioned it, I'm sure you would have been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me then that in February of 1998 you never mentioned Colonel Beara to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. If it's not in the transcript, then I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that in February 1998 you didn't say a thing to Mr. Ruez about the meeting that you allegedly had with these two officers on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you also agree with me that in February 1998 you also didn't say anything to Mr. Ruez about the fact that some machines were required from you, that something to that effect was asked from you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never asked me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Very well, but who asked you that? Who did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The first time ever. When was it the first time you were ever asked about that? *A. I suppose that it was Karnavas in the Blagojevic case. I really can't remember. I'm saying "perhaps" or "probably." I'm not sure who was the first to ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we are also redacting. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the first time you mentioned that was as a Defence witness in Blagojevic? On page -- on the side of Colonel Blagojevic, actually.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I'm not sure, but I'm sure that I was telling the truth. That's what I'm sure of. When, where I said it for the first time, I really can't be of -- sure of that. But I adhere by what I said. It is possible that it was then when I mentioned it the first time. I'm not sure, I don't want to speculate. But I did say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the Defence case of Mr. Blagojevic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What was the Defence case of Mr. Blagojevic, that he was not in the area at the time and that the security officers are responsible for whatever happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because nothing of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He made it before us, actually. So your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go back into open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to open session then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about DM, can you tell us, please, what was your relationship, relationship between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two people with the same initials, DM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The one who was director.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had a good relationship. We resided in the same place, we were the same generation, we were friends before the war, during the war, we are still friends and peers. We cooperated, he was the director of the public utility company, and the founder of the municipality, and we had an extremely good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: You are talking about your personal relationship. What about your professional relationship? Did he report to you, was it he responsible to you, i.e., the institution that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it came to the supply of the city with water and also when it came to garbage collection. In those two respects he was responsible to the municipality and to the Executive Board. When it came to the municipal utilities this was within the purview of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When you say that you also imply the use of some machinery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only if they are used to repair the mains, the water infrastructure, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about regular maintenance, regular circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What about extraordinary circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's extraordinary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: For example, natural disasters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: War operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the public utilities and the civilians' protection would intervene together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And what about war operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down, please. You're running too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: War operations, the engagement of machinery in war operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that they were responsible before the Executive Board, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Also, who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence and the secretariat for national defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So we're now talking legalities here. In your personal and professional relationship that was very close, as far as I understood you, did that person inform you about any of his activities during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: He didn't say a thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: That he had some meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I am asking you as a person who was an official, in case the machinery was involved in any activities, especially the machinery that belonged to the public utilities, would that require a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: A report on the work within that institution, within that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might have been a report. Maybe a report was drafted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you whether that would be a customary thing, to draft a report, on the use of such machinery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be a paper trail on everything. If a piece of machinery was used, then there would also be fuel used and there should be a paper trail to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What about locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not director of that company. I wouldn't know. I did not have any machinery at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about your relationship with Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. Would you agree with me that Miroslav Deronjic was factually the power-wielder in Bratunac, that all the power was in his hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you partly. Miroslav Deronjic was the number one person in Bratunac with the highest authority, most influence. I can't say that everybody asked him about everything a hundred per cent of the things, but he had the say in quite a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with him in the political sense, in the sense of the organisation of the civilian powers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we were neighbours. Our -- we are -- we were first-door neighbours. I am a bit older than him. We were very good neighbours; very, very good neighbours. I can't say that we shared the same political opinions. He joined the SDS at the beginning of multi-party system, and I was with the SDP and it was only 1996 that I joined the SDS. However, irrespective of that, we had a good relationship. We respected each other's opinions. He had more influence. We all respected him and we held him in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I'll be able to wrap up this topic within a minute. It will be my suggestion that we have our next break now. Are we in private session? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's time to have a break. So you will continue your cross-examination in 25 minutes' time, Mr. Mrkic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, before you continue, Mr. Mrkic, Judge Stole cannot be with us for the last session, due to unavoidable reasons. So we are proceeding pursuant to Rule 15 bis (A). Yes, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we have started with this topic in private session, I would like to ask to return to private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's revert to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship with Mr. Deronjic in political terms? Was he your superior, were you obliged to listen to his orders, instructions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1996 he was my superior, because that was when I joined the SDS. Before that, I was not in the party, however the party put me forward, even though I wasn't a member, for the post of president of the Executive Board in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: In 1994, when you came to that post, did you receive any orders from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't really our superior; it wasn't his practice. We had our own board. It was a seven-member body, and we wouldn't be making all the decisions. Sometimes he would attend these conferences, if some topic of interest would be on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 2D81. The English version is on page 11, lines 29 to 33, and in Serbian, page 12, lines two to six. This is the English -- this is the Serbian version. Can we please split the screen so that we can have both versions on the monitor? Can we scroll down the English version, please? The Serbian version is fine. These are lines 29 to 33 in English, and in Serbian, lines two to six.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: In the interview that you gave to Mr. Ruez, you said, amongst other things, that you received orders directly from Deronjic because Deronjic was in charge of civilian affairs in the town, and he was appointed by the president himself, and that you had no contact with the army and they did not issue orders to you, the army. They followed their line of work, and you followed your civilian line of work. If you can explain, please, what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is understood for that period of the 11th, 12th, the 13th and the 14th, at the time Deronjic was appointed by President Karadzic as the commissioner for civilian affairs for the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. This did not refer to the period before the 11th of July, 1995. I think that this is clear now, isn't it? During the Srebrenica operation, during that period, he was appointed, and he was the person -- well, perhaps I wasn't precise enough here regarding that contact with the military. We still had contacts with them through the logistics deputy in terms of supplying the brigade with food, cigarettes, and so on. This is something that was in the -- part of the duties of the Executive Board. But during the actual operation, we didn't have any contacts with the military, we didn't participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I'm interested in. It says here that we received orders directly from Deronjic. If we put that in the context of the 11th of July, 1995, onwards, Mr. Deronjic was performing this post, he was appointed to by President Karadzic. What kind of orders did you receive from Deronjic? Can you please answer that first and then I will would move to my next question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not thinking of anything particular. Perhaps I was imprecise here when talking to Mr. Ruez. There were no particular orders. We didn't do anything in particular, we just made sure that the town had electricity, water, that the children went to school, that the shops were supplied; that was our job. So that was when we were perhaps receiving some sort of suggestion or an order from Deronjic, but we didn't receive any particular orders in terms of the military. We were simply dealing with the normal functioning of things in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Does that imply that you were not obliged, if you did receive an order from the military, to carry out that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could only receive a request from the army, practically the brigade needs 100 uniforms, for example. It needs 500 packs of cigarettes, and all we could say was we have that and we can do or we don't have it and we cannot do it. The army needs a hundred litres of oil, for example, cooking oil; we have it. This is the kind of thing -- this kind of thing that has to do with logistic supplies of food, clothing, cigarettes, and fuel. If petrol station had any and the army needed a tonne of fuel, we either had it or didn't have it. It was clear what sort of demands or requests the military made to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you about requests, I was asking you about orders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the army did not issue orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And what about war prisoners, prisoners of war, what was your relationship with the army in that sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness can be shown Exhibit P -- from the 65 ter list, P10, Exhibit P10. We are still in private session. This is a decision on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica signed by the President of the Republic, Radoslav -- Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to Article 4, and if we can comment on that, please. Specifically, in the context that we have just talked about. Paragraph 4 says, "The commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to." You have just stated that, in terms of prisoners of war, civilian organs did not have any jurisdiction. Through this decision, at least it does not seem so to me. So can you please comment on this decision. From what I understood, you are aware of the existence of this decision, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of it, but I'm not actually aware of it. This does not concern the municipality of Bratunac, but the municipality of Serbian Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about the prisoners of war from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision appointing Deronjic as commissioner for civilian affairs of the municipality of Serbian Srebrenica is just that. But it does not refer to Bratunac, the municipality of Bratunac and its own organs. It had its own president and it is stated here very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: That's not the problem. I'm just placing that in the context of what you told Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had nothing to do with prisoners of war. Please, and -- please don't ask me about that. I am very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because you, in your testimony, said that in front of the buses that were in Bratunac there were civilian policemen. I'm also asking you because you, in your testimony, said that people from civilian structures, you don't know who, sent retired persons to the playing fields and the schools, if I understood that correctly, to make it seem as if the security was stronger, because the situation was unsafe. So I'm talking about prisoners of war from Srebrenica. I'm talking about how Mr. Miroslav Deronjic was appointed as civilian commissioner with the duties we have just mentioned, and I'm talking about that. And my question is too long.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any sense in what you're asking. I don't know what you mean when you say "civilian policemen." There is a term, military police, these are people with white cross-belts and green camouflage uniforms. We also have the civilian police, if that is the correct name. They have blue camouflage uniforms, and if that's the kind of police that you are thinking of. I don't know what you mean when you say civilian police. These are members of the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And under whose jurisdiction are they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: And in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, under the jurisdiction of the ministry of internal affairs. There is no third type of police. I know about two kinds of police, military police, which is in the army, and there is the civilian police which is under the ministry for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will hear the next -- please move to another topic or area please, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Since we are still in private session, I would like to go back to your meeting of the 14th of July, 1995. I would just like to ask you what was the name of the secretary who called you to come to the municipal offices of the SDS on the 14th of July in the morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name is Mirna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what her last name is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was single then; she wasn't married.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: You either know it or you don't know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Nikolic. I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I think her name is Mirna. I know her father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead, if you can give us as many particulars as you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Milorad, her father, he worked in the Jasanic forestry service. That was it. She's now married and lives in Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you if you remember the person that you spoke with and who introduced himself as Colonel Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you describe that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that person here now. And the face has changed a lot. At the time he looked very different, more vigorous, younger, in a better mood. I don't know. Had I not known that it was Colonel Beara, I would not have recognised him if I saw him in the street. I still have -- or I still remember him as what -- what he looked like then. I wouldn't recognise him now in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it is Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: I regularly follow "The Hague Diary" broadcast, which is shown for half an hour every Saturday, so I see many faces. I'm familiar with the Trial Chamber, with many persons from the Registry, the Prosecution. I know all these faces from seeing them on television. I've seen His Honour Judge Agius in the Blagojevic case, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I must have looked very different then, because I -- I wasn't on the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Deronjic case. Well, in any case, I know your face very well, and you look very good and you don't change that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to another subject, Mr. Mrkic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the meeting that was held on the 14th. The two officers -- but let's first confirm one thing. Mr. Beara did not enter with you, the person who introduced himself as Colonel Beara didn't enter with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he stayed in the office where I found him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness and Mr. Mrkic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't finish my question and he already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not your fault, it's the witness, actually. But please allow a short pause between question and answer. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] See if I understand the situation well, in that other office you were there with the two officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Was that the office belonging to the person that we have just spoken about? We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: MD, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Where was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The two officers in question with whom you spoke and who never introduced themselves to you, and you don't know which unit they belonged to, were they at the Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. I wouldn't say that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So you saw them for the first time at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: The person who you think was Colonel Ljubisa Beara, did you see him before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at the Fontana?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: When you said that a driver was required for that piece of machinery, if I understand your testimony well, was it one of the officer who told you that he would be providing a driver for that machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We never mentioned any drivers. I was the one who mentioned that, because I thought a man has to go with the machinery. Maybe they had somebody in the military, but that was my conclusion, if a piece of equipment was required, then a man should accompany that piece of equipment. And this person used that piece of equipment, and that's why I thought he would accompany the machine. They never mentioned the person who would be handling the machine, none of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: What was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a stormy reaction. One of them was very aggressive when he said, "It's not up to you to say who can handle the machine and who can't." And we stopped at that. I apologised. I said this was just a remark, you have no obligations towards me, and that's how the conversation ended. And let me just tell you this: When I went to that office, when I left the SDS premises, I spoke to the director of the brickworks on the phone, and the machinery belonged to him, and I told him that people from the military would come and that he should give them the machine. Whether the people came to fetch the machine, whether he gave it to them, I don't know. I never investigated. I don't know whether the machine was ever given to these people or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Something else I would like to know about that. Which of the two officers told you that it was not up to you to ponder that issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Colonel, lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know. He was very fresh with me and I was hardly waiting to leave the room. I didn't know anybody. I didn't know any of them. If I knew their names, then I would maybe shed some light on that, but I didn't know any of the names. I wouldn't be able to put any names to any of the faces, so I couldn't care less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever tell anybody about the meeting that you had after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anything to the person that we discussed a while ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: MD? No. I just called the director and told him what I told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to another situation, which took place in 1992. We confirmed that in 1992, in the same school where the detainees were kept in 1995, the detainees were also kept there in 1992. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, but I only know it as a private person. At that time, I was not in any position in the municipality. I was just a foot soldier; I had been mobilised to the army. I heard about that, that this lasted for a few days in Bratunac, but I never went to the school myself. At the time, I was not involved in politics. I was not in any position. I was just a foot soldier. And it was not of any interest to me. I just heard about it in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: So you said this about the school. Let me ask you, according to what you know, whether in 1992, Muslims were also kept in the playground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims? Don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only -- I apologise. May I? It is only now that we hear about graves being discovered, bodies being unearthed, but I myself don't know where burials took place, who was buried, and this is something that is being done now, and you can read about it in -- in the press and watch it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me when I say that during that period this was still localised, at a local level, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Bratunac municipality. I don't know what the situation was like in other municipalities. I suppose that Bratunac was not alone in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please consult with my colleagues just for a moment, if you can bear with me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify a few more things. In the interview that you gave to Mr. Ruez, you mentioned that you had some notes. If you want me, I can find that in Exhibit Number 2D81, page number 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we are going to remain in open session, then I suggest that, if it's shown up on the monitor, it's not broadcast and we can remain in open session. Unless you prefer to go in private session, in which case we would grant you that as well. You choose, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we can stay in open session, but the document should not be displayed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you're asking me. But go ahead, ask me. I assume what you're going to say. I know why I said this to Ruez. I suppose that he asked me about some events, about some dates that I was not sure about, that I didn't know, and I suppose -- actually, I know that I told him that I could check that. I did not have any particular notes at work. I had an agenda where I entered various dates. For example, on the 8th of February, I had a to-do list and I ticked the boxes of the things that were done. That's what I meant when I said that I had notes. In that agenda book, there were dates and entries that could have jogged my memory. I did not keep a war diary, if that's what I mean. I did not have any special notes. I'm sorry that I didn't, actually. I don't -- I'm not saying that I wish for the things to repeat, but I didn't keep a diary at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well I -- I may have jumped the gun. I might -- I thought that you -- you were after this, after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. Perhaps you do realise yourself that in this case maybe you are running, and running fast. I would suggest to you that you wait until you hear the question that is put to you, and then answer the question and nothing but the question. Because otherwise you're going to be here for days and days. And it's in everybody's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because we also received from our learned friend from the Prosecution another set of notes. I would just like to see with you whether we are talking about the same set of notes or a different set of notes. Did you make some notes recently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I made some notes here at the Tribunal when I was listening to the tape of *my testimony in the Blagojevic case, and I made notes of some dates and these are the notes that I gave to the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor took those notes from me. I believe that this is the set of notes that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: In other words, those are not the notes that you mentioned in the interview with Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. Those are the notes that I made two days ago, not those that I made in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I've noticed two things in that set of notes. Maybe we could talk about that. First of all, did you note the most important things or the things that you remember the best?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had known that it would reach your hands, I would not have made any notes at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness. Witness. Again, once more, I have to remind you to please allow Mr. Mrkic, and for that matter, every our lawyer that will be cross-examining you later on, to finish their question first before you start jumping in with your answer. Okay? Mr. Mrkic, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Again, thank you. Mr. Mrkic's cross-examination has been going on for too long. And -- and if I had known that these notes would ever reach either the Prosecution or him, I would never have made them. I just kept the notes for myself. I might have been imprecise or ambiguous, but what can I do now? It has reached your hands. Go ahead, fire away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mrkic. We've got six, seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and finish within that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you then. Why are you against either me or some other colleagues of mine looking at these notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've talked about everything. I just made a note of some dates to jog my own memory. I am not bothered. I apologise for having said it at all. I'm not bothered by the fact that you are aware of my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Is it because under 14 July 1995 you have noted that you were invited by the SDS secretary to come to the SDS and that you met up with Colonel Beara when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: But there is nothing in your notes about the meeting that you had with the two officers and what they had asked you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just a reminder. I knew that this happened at the time. I did not have to remind myself of that. This is a reminder, a note, for myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't believe the witness has a copy of the notes, and perhaps, you know, I have a copy of them, and I could furnish it to them, but I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that Mr. Mrkic gives him his back, and then we can move to another topic. Do you want to pursue this line of questions on his notes, or not, Mr. Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two or three questions and then I will move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have found a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, by all means. Just show it to Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Mrkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: Are these the notes that you kept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was in one notebook, and now this is a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If you can look at the part that refers to the 14th of July, 1995, please. I think it's the one but last page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in what you wrote later, or afterwards, at the end. Could you please read that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I take it? I repeat again, this was just a kind of summary for me, and I wrote this at the end in order to just remind myself. Let me read that. I did not inform anyone about the situation in Bratunac because I did not have any communication, either with the government or the assembly. I think that it was the duty of MD, because he was appointed as commissioner by the President for the municipality of Srebrenica. This is something that I said already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If I can put a question to you now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you made these notes to have a reminder about the events by the dates in the sequence that they took place. So what is the purpose of this commentary at the end? It's not a reminder of the events or of any facts. It's not a reminder -- well, sincerely speaking, this seems like a justification to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A justification for whom? For me. Not to me. For me, it's still a reminder so that I can tell the Tribunal what I wrote, but perhaps differently. I mean, this is just a reminder for me stating that during the Srebrenica operation I had no communication at all with the state leadership, either in the government or the political leadership, and that this communication, if anybody had such communication, was -- it was Deronjic. I, or the municipal assembly president, LJS, did not communicate, we did not have a prime minister, a president of the assembly or anyone. So it was just a reminder for me. It's not a justification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop here for the day, Mr. Mrkic, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MRKIC
utterances.text: That's my suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, look at me. It's very important, and I'm telling you this in a most serious manner possible, that between now and when you finish your testimony, you do not communicate with anyone. And when I say anyone, that includes other possible witnesses, on the subject matter of your testimony. Similarly, not to allow anyone to contact you or discuss matters related to your testimony here. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I understand, and I am not communicating with anyone in -- about my testimony. As for the fact that we are accommodated all together in the hotel, all the witnesses, well, then, you should have put us up in different hotels, so that we don't see each other at all. But we don't talk about testimony, we just sit in the lobby, in the dining-room, we talk about football, travel, about The Hague, where we were, what we did. Otherwise we should be put in different hotels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enough. I think the witness can -- I think we can finish here today and we will continue tomorrow. We stand adjourned until 9.00 tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
